# Introduction
Financial markets do not behave consistently over time, as periods of growth, decline, stability, and high volatility can occur under different market conditions.
To describe these market conditions more precisely, we define three market regimes: bull, bear and consolidation/sideways.
A bear market regime occurs when stock prices decline by 20% or more from a recent peak over a sustained period of time.
A bull market regime occurs when stock prices rise 20% or more from a recent low over a sustained period of time.
A sideways market regime occurs when stock prices fluctuate up and down within a narrow range.
An important distinction is that these market regimes are not directly observable. 
We can observe stock prices and returns, but we cannot directly observe whether the market is currently in a bull, bear, or sideways regime.

Due to the "hidden" nature of the stock market regimes, Hidden Markov Models provide a helpful framework for identifying and analysing these unobservable regimes.
Hidden Markov models can be used to identify the likelihood of moving between market regimes and the signals given by the market (stock-prices) that define each state.
The primary objective of this project is to use both simulated and real-world stock-market data to fit a Hidden Markov Model, and interpret the characteristics and transition probabilities of the regimes it identifies.

The rest of this project is as follows. Section 2 reviews the theory of Markov chains and Hidden Markov Models.
Section 3 presents the simulation study and real stock-market data application (all code and outputs will be in an Appendix).
Section 4 summarizes the main findings and limitations of the project, followed by References in section 5.





# Review of the Topic

A Hidden Markov Model is a model where we observe a sequence of emissions, in this case stock market returns; however, the sequence of states the model went through to generate these emissions is unknown, i.e., hidden.
In our project, the hidden states are stock market regimes, as we cannot directly observe them but must instead infer them from stock market data.
Hidden Markov Models are built on the theory of Markov Chains, i.e. the hidden states follow the Markov assumption.
To understand how HMMs can be applied to stock market regime detection, we first review the fundamentals of Markov chains, then introduce Hidden Markov Models and their applications to stock markets.


## Markov Chains
A markov chain models transition between states under the assumption of the Markov property.
$$
P(X_{t+1}=j\mid X_t=i).
$$
The transition probabilties are modelled by the transition matrix (P) which is defined as:
$$
P_{ij}=P(X_{t+1}=j\mid X_t=i),
\qquad
\sum_j P_{ij}=1.
$$
For the purpose of this project, we will be using a finite state, time-homogeneous Markov chain. The states in the Markov Chain will represent stock market regimes i.e. bull, bear and sideways (finite-state Markov chain).
The transition matrix for our project will define the probabilities of moving between these states over time.

## Hidden Markov Models
Hidden Markov Models are an extension of the Markov Chain framework where the underlying states are unobservable i.e. hidden and can only be inferred through observable data.
Each of the underlying "hidden" states generates output according to a probability distribution which is known as the emission distribution. The outputs generated by the states are directly observable.
In our project the hidden states we aim to identify are as follows: bull, bear, and sideways, i.e. the hidden states represent market regimes, and the observations from each hidden state we collect are stock market returns.

Hidden Markov Models have 3 main components:
1. Transition Matrix (A): Represents the probabilities of transitioning between hidden states.
2. Emission Distribution (B): Describes the probability distribution of stock market returns (observed value) within each hidden state.
3. Initial distribution($\pi$): Represents the probability of starting in a hidden regime
These 3 components together define a Hidden Markov Model: $$\lambda = (A, B, \pi)$$.
Visually, the Hidden Markov Model looks as such:

```{r hmm-diagram, echo=FALSE, dev="pdf", fig.width=9, fig.height=4.2, fig.align="center", fig.cap="Structure of a Hidden Markov Model"}
par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0), xpd = NA)
plot.new()
plot.window(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 5))

x <- c(2.5, 5, 7.5)
top <- 3.8
bottom <- 1.5

# Hidden states
for (i in seq_along(x)) {
  rect(x[i] - 0.65, top - 0.4, x[i] + 0.65, top + 0.4,
       col = "white", border = "black")
  text(x[i], top, paste0("X", i), cex = 1.2)

  rect(x[i] - 0.65, bottom - 0.4, x[i] + 0.65, bottom + 0.4,
       col = "white", border = "black")
  text(x[i], bottom, paste0("Y", i), cex = 1.2)
}

# State transitions
for (i in 1:2) {
  arrows(x[i] + 0.7, top, x[i + 1] - 0.7, top,
         length = 0.12)
  text(mean(x[i:(i + 1)]), top + 0.25, "A")
}

# Emissions
for (i in seq_along(x)) {
  arrows(x[i], top - 0.45, x[i], bottom + 0.45,
         length = 0.12)
  text(x[i] + 0.25, 2.65, "B")
}

text(0.6, top, "Hidden\nstates", cex = 0.9)
text(0.6, bottom, "Observed\nreturns", cex = 0.9)
```
The horizontal arrows represent transitions between hidden states which are based on the transition matrix A.
The vertical arrows represent observations generated by each state according to the emission distribution B.

Since stock market returns are continuous observations, our project models the emission distributions using a Gaussian distribution.
In the Gaussian distribution each hidden state i.e. market regime has a mean and variance.
The use of the Gaussian emission distribution for hidden states is defined mathematically as:
$$
Y_t \mid X_t=i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2)
$$
- $Y_t$: observed stock market return at time $t$
- $X_t=i$: the hidden state $i$ the market is currently in
- $\mu_i$: mean of stock market returns in state $i$
- $\sigma_i^2$: variance of stock market returns in state $i$







## Details of the topic
This is a mathematical formua without formula number.
$$h(x) = \frac{f(x)}{S(x)} = -\frac{d \log[S(x])}{\rm dx}$$
 
 
This is how write a fomula and label it. 
\begin{align}
\label{eq2}
S(x) = \exp[-H(x)] = \exp[-\int_0^x h(u) {\rm d}u]
\end{align}
